topic: PAYMENTS, TAX & COMPLIANCE for a GTA (Ontario) sole proprietor selling AI-built digital subscriptions worldwide in late 2026, with an AI running the business and the owner spending ≤10h once and ≤3h/week. Covers the payment rail (Stripe Canada vs merchant-of-record vs app stores), GST/HST small-supplier rules (ETA s.148 fetched), foreign VAT (EU, UK, Korea), CASL, PIPEDA for chat data, AI disclosure, refund/cancellation rules, and the EI interaction (EI Regs s.30 minor extent, s.19(2), s.36(6.1)). Method: federal statutes were read directly from the justicecanada/laws-lois-xml XML (ETA current to 2026-06-21; CASL to 2026-03-02; PIPEDA, Competition Act and IRPA to 2026-03-31; EI Regs to 2026-04-28; EI Act to 2026-06-21). Korean statutes came from the legalize-kr/legalize-kr GitHub mirror of law.go.kr. Vendor facts came from official vendor repos (Polar) or dated 2026 secondary GitHub documents. WebSearch was not used.

key_facts.fact: ETA s.148(1) (verbatim core): a person is a small supplier 'throughout a particular calendar quarter and the first month immediately following' it if the consideration that 'became due… or was paid' in 'the four calendar quarters immediately preceding' it, for 'taxable supplies… made inside or outside Canada', does 'not exceed… $30,000'. s.148(2): if the total within a single calendar quarter exceeds $30,000, small-supplier status ends 'immediately before that time'. Because the test counts supplies made 'inside or outside Canada', worldwide sales count, including foreign ones.

ETA s.123(1): 'taxable supply means a supply that is made in the course of a commercial activity'; 'zero-rated supply means a supply included in Schedule VI'. Zero-rated exports are therefore still taxable supplies and count toward the $30,000 test.

ETA s.166: while a person is 'a small supplier who is not a registrant', the consideration 'shall not be included in calculating the tax payable', so no GST/HST is charged. s.240(1)(a) exempts small suppliers from mandatory registration. s.240(2.1)(b): once no longer a small supplier, the person must apply 'before the day that is 30 days after… the day the person first makes a taxable supply in Canada, otherwise than as a small supplier'. s.240(3) allows voluntary registration. s.242(2) (per cross_compliance): cancellation is possible only after at least 1 year of registration.

ETA s.142(1)(c)(i): a supply of intangible personal property is deemed made in Canada if 'the property may be used in whole or in part in Canada'. s.142(1)(g): a service is deemed made in Canada if it 'is, or is to be, performed in whole or in part in Canada'. A software licence or subscription usable anywhere, supplied by a Canadian resident, is therefore generally a supply made in Canada; it can then be zero-rated as an export.

ETA Schedule VI Part V (exports). s.10 zero-rates a licence to use IP where 'the recipient is a non-resident person who is not registered under Subdivision D of Division V'. s.10.1 zero-rates IPP to such an unregistered non-resident, except a supply 'to an individual unless the individual is outside Canada at that time' and IPP 'that may only be used in Canada'. s.7 zero-rates services to non-residents but excludes individuals in Canada and 'advisory, consulting or professional' services (those are covered by s.23). Consequence: a sale to a non-resident merchant of record is zero-rated under s.10/10.1 only if that MoR is NOT normally GST-registered (Subdivision D).

ETA s.211.13 (digital economy): the rule that deems a distribution platform operator to be the supplier applies only to a 'specified non-resident supplier', defined as 'a non-resident person that does not make supplies in the course of a business carried on in Canada and that is not registered under Subdivision D'. A Canadian-resident developer selling through the App Store or Google Play is NOT covered by this statutory deeming rule.

ETA Schedule VIII lists Ontario at 8%. With GST at 5% under s.165(1), Ontario HST is 13%. The same schedule text lists Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Newfoundland at 8%, which does not match the rates I recall [prior knowledge, unverified, pre-2026-06: NB/NL/PEI 15% HST total, NS 14% from April 2025]. Those rates appear to be set outside Schedule VIII, so non-Ontario HST rates are unverified.

EI Regs s.30(1): in any week a claimant 'is self-employed or engaged in the operation of a business on the claimant's own account', they are 'considered to have worked a full working week'. s.30(2): the exception is a business run 'to such a minor extent that a person would not normally rely on that… engagement as a principal means of livelihood'. s.30(3) factors: (a) time spent; (b) capital and resources invested; (c) financial success or failure; (d) continuity; (e) nature of the business; (f) intention and willingness to seek and immediately accept other employment. The test asks whether the claimant is operating a business, not whether they personally do the work, so an AI-run business is still their business.

EI Regs s.36(6.1): self-employment earnings 'that arise from a transaction' are allocated (b) 'to the week in which the transaction occurred' if that week's total is at most the maximum yearly insurable earnings ÷ 52. If the total is higher, (a) they are allocated to the weeks in which the work was performed. s.36(6) allocates earnings from services to the weeks the services were performed. s.35(10)(c): self-employment income is gross income minus operating expenses (per cross_compliance). Subscription sales would therefore generally land in the week they occur.

EI Act s.19(2): after the waiting period, benefits are reduced by 50% of earnings up to 90% of weekly insurable earnings and by 100% above that. s.38(1)(c): the Commission may penalize a claimant who 'knowingly failed to declare… all or some of the claimant's earnings'. s.18(1)(a): the claimant must be 'capable of and available for work'. Pilot Project 24 measures cover benefit periods beginning up to 2026-10-10; no extension was found. The 2026 maximum weekly benefit is about $729 (secondary source plus formula check).

CASL s.6(1)–(2): every commercial electronic message (CEM) needs consent plus sender identification, contact information and an unsubscribe mechanism. s.6(6): messages that 'solely' facilitate or confirm a transaction (b), give factual notice about an ongoing 'subscription, membership, account' (d), or deliver product updates (f) are exempt only from paragraph (1)(a), the consent requirement. They must still carry the identification and unsubscribe content required by s.6(2).

CASL s.10(10): an existing business relationship arises from (a) a purchase 'within the two-year period' before the message, or (e) 'an inquiry or application, within the six-month period'. s.10(14)(a): for 'ongoing use or ongoing purchase under a subscription', the 2-year period begins 'on the day that the subscription… terminates'. s.10(1): an express-consent request must state its purposes and identify the requester. s.13: the sender bears the onus of proving consent.

CASL s.12(1): 'A person contravenes section 6 only if a computer system located in Canada is used to send or access the electronic message.' Marketing email sent from Canada to foreign users is therefore covered. s.11: the unsubscribe must be free, stay valid for 60 days and be honoured within 10 business days. The maximum penalty is $1M for an individual (s.20(4), per cross_compliance). SOR/2012-36 s.2(1)(d) requires a mailing address in every CEM.

CASL s.8(1): a person must not, 'in the course of a commercial activity, install or cause to be installed a computer program on any other person's computer system' without express consent. s.10(8) deems consent for cookies, HTML and JavaScript where conduct shows consent, and s.10(7) covers consented updates. This is relevant to any downloadable app or extension that the owner installs or updates.

PIPEDA s.4(1)(a) covers personal information collected 'in the course of commercial activities'. s.5(3) limits purposes to those 'a reasonable person would consider are appropriate'. s.6.1: consent is valid only if the individual 'would understand the nature, purpose and consequences'. Schedule 1: 4.1.3 the organization remains responsible for information 'transferred to a third party for processing' and must use 'contractual or other means' to protect it; 4.2 purposes must be identified 'at or before the time' of collection; 4.5.3 information no longer needed 'should be destroyed, erased, or made anonymous'; 4.7 safeguards must be 'appropriate to the sensitivity'; 4.8.2(a) the name or title and address of the accountable person must be made available. Breach reporting and a 24-month breach record: s.10.1 and SOR/2018-64 (per cross_compliance).

No enacted federal Canadian AI-disclosure or replacement privacy statute was found. GitHub code search of justicecanada/laws-lois-xml returned 0 hits for 'Consumer Privacy Protection Act' and 'Artificial Intelligence and Data Act', against 1 hit for PIPEDA. This is weak evidence, because very large files may not be indexed. [prior knowledge, unverified, pre-2026-06: Bill C-27 died on the order paper in January 2025.]

Competition Act s.74.01(1)(a): a representation to the public that is 'false or misleading in a material respect' is reviewable conduct. s.74.01(1.1), drip pricing: a price 'not attainable due to fixed obligatory charges or fees' is misleading 'unless the obligatory charges or fees represent only an amount imposed… by or under an Act', which covers taxes. s.74.1(1)(c)(i): the penalty for an individual is up to the greater of $750,000 ($1,000,000 for subsequent orders) and three times the benefit. Fake AI-generated testimonials, or presenting a bot as a human consultant, fall under this section.

IRPA s.91(1): 'no person shall knowingly, directly or indirectly, represent or advise a person for consideration… in connection with… a proceeding or application under this Act', unless they are a lawyer, paralegal, Quebec notary or CICC member (s.91(2)). s.91(9): the penalty is up to $200,000 and/or 2 years on indictment, or $40,000 and/or 6 months on summary conviction. This corrects the secondary '$50k–$100k' figure in cand_korean.json. A paid AI immigration-consultation bot falls squarely inside s.91(1).

ITA Part XX (s.282) platform reporting: 'relevant activity' means a 'relevant service' (rental of real property, a 'personal service', or rental of a means of transport) or 'the sale of goods', and 'goods means any tangible property'. Selling software or digital subscriptions through an MoR or app store is therefore not a reportable relevant activity. The income is still taxable and self-reported on T2125: file by June 15, pay by April 30 (per cross_compliance).

Stripe Canada, SECONDARY (the official page was blocked): 2.9% + C$0.30 per domestic card, plus 0.8% for international cards (one source says +1.0%) and 2% for currency conversion. Stripe Billing costs 0.7% and Stripe Tax 0.5%. With plain Stripe the owner is the merchant, so tax registration and remittance, disputes and support remain the owner's job. Stripe Tax calculates tax but does not register the seller.

Stripe Managed Payments (Stripe as merchant of record) costs '3.5% per successful Managed Payments transaction in addition to Payments fees' (capture of Stripe's US pricing page, 2026-06-04). Secondary sources report general availability since 2026-04-22, AI services eligible since 2026-06-02, Canadian sellers supported, and an eligibility review that excludes 'professional-service/consulting offers'. The Canadian rate was not found. A search snippet from Paddle's page (competitor claim, undated) says it does not support customers in South Korea.

Paddle (merchant of record): 5% + $0.50, all-inclusive of tax and currency conversion; products priced under $10 need a 'custom discussion' (secondary, 2026-09-19, citing paddle.com/pricing). Lemon Squeezy: Stripe acquired it in July 2024 (secondary, 2026-06-21, and [prior knowledge, unverified, pre-2026-06]). Its January 28, 2026 update describes moving toward Stripe Managed Payments with slower updates and no published shutdown deadline. Fees are 5% + $0.50, plus 0.5% on subscriptions, 1.5% on international cards and 1.5% on PayPal.

Polar (merchant of record; official docs repo): Starter costs 5% + 50¢, plus 1.5% on international cards and $15 per dispute. Payouts cost $2 per month plus 0.25% + $0.25 each, plus up to 1% cross-border. Fees are not returned on refunds. Polar may refund customers at its discretion for up to 60 days and may suspend accounts whose chargeback rate approaches about 0.7%.

Polar Acceptable Use Policy (effective 2026-03-25, official repo). PROHIBITED: 'Human services'; 'AI relationship services'; 'Services used by, intended for, or advertised towards minors'; 'loot boxes'; 'Fake testimonials, reviews'; 'financial advice… related to tax guidance'; 'Medical and Health advice'; 'clairvoyance, horoscopes, fortune-telling'; 'Regulated services'. CLOSER REVIEW, may be refused: 'AI Content Generation tools', 'chatbot generators', 'Spiritual & Astrology services', 'eBooks'. A fortune-telling (saju) or AI-companion product is therefore likely refused on Polar. Paddle's and Stripe's policies on these categories were not checked.

Stripe payout timing (docs mirror): the first payout is typically 7–14 days after the first payment. The settlement table lists Canada at 7 days for the first payout and 3 business days after that. Stripe Tax supports Canada as a business location and South Korea as a customer location (digital products).

App stores, SECONDARY (2026-08-14, citing Apple and Google pages): Apple charges 30% on year-1 subscriptions and 15% after a subscriber's first paid year. The Small Business Program charges 15% from day one for developers under $1M of proceeds, starting '15 days after the end of the fiscal month of approval'. Google Play charges 10% service + 5% billing = 15% on the first $1M for recurring products in the US/UK/EEA from 2026-06-30; the Canadian rollout is not confirmed. Google Play registration costs $25 once. [prior knowledge, unverified, pre-2026-06: the Apple Developer Program costs US$99/year, and digital subscriptions sold inside iOS/Android apps on the Canadian storefront must use store billing.]

EU VAT (SECONDARY, openaccountants skill, 2026-07-13, pending review): sellers outside the EU get no threshold. They must charge destination-country VAT on every B2C digital sale from the first one and use the non-Union OSS or register in each member state. Customer location needs two pieces of non-contradictory evidence. A marketplace or platform may be the 'deemed supplier' (Implementing Regulation 282/2011 Art 9a).

Korea VAT Act art. 53-2(1): a foreign business supplying 'electronic services' to Korea over networks must complete simplified registration 'within 20 days of the start of business'. Covered services include games, audio and video files and software (item 1), advertising (2) and cloud computing (3); supplies to registered Korean businesses are excluded. The statutory text states no threshold. art. 53-2(2): where the service is supplied through a third party that runs an open market, or that collects payment from the buyer and pays the seller, that third party is deemed the supplier and must register. art. 30: the rate is 10%. art. 53-2(6): transaction records must be kept for 5 years.

UK VAT [prior knowledge, unverified, pre-2026-06]: a business with no UK establishment that sells digital services to UK consumers must register for UK VAT from its first sale (no threshold for non-established sellers); standard rate 20%. US [prior knowledge, unverified, pre-2026-06]: state sales-tax 'economic nexus' thresholds are typically $100,000 of sales (some states also 200 transactions) per state, and whether SaaS or digital goods are taxable varies by state.

Korea e-Commerce Consumer Protection Act (version in force 2026-07-21). art. 17(1): 7-day withdrawal right. art. 17(2)5 removes it once digital-content provision has begun, but only if the seller clearly marks that and provides a trial (art. 17(6)). art. 13(6): before a subscription price increase or a free-to-paid conversion, the seller must obtain the consumer's consent and give notice of how to cancel. art. 21-2(1) prohibits: showing only part of the total price on the first screen (1); pre-checked opt-ins (2); visually misleading choice buttons (3); cancellation flows more complex than signup, or cancellation only by a different method (4); repeated pop-ups pressing the consumer to reverse a decision (5).

Canadian refund and cancellation rules, SECONDARY (a 2026 code module; ontario.ca was blocked): Ontario's Consumer Protection Act, 2023 replaced the 2002 Act on 2026-01-01 and adds rules on unilateral amendment and renewal. Every province prohibits negative-option billing. Quebec CPA ss.54.1–54.16 give a cancellation right for distance contracts that lacked required disclosure, plus a statutory chargeback against the card issuer. The Ontario CPA 2023's specific remote-agreement and subscription-cancellation sections were NOT verified.

EU consumer rules, SECONDARY: Directive (EU) 2023/2673 requires a prominent 'withdrawal button/function' for contracts concluded online, applicable from 19 June 2026; the path must be as simple as signup and state the 14-day withdrawal period. [prior knowledge, unverified, pre-2026-06: for digital content, the 14-day right is lost only if the consumer gives express consent plus acknowledgement before supply begins. The US FTC click-to-cancel rule was vacated by the 8th Circuit in July 2025; California's auto-renewal law still applies to California consumers.]

Anthropic Usage Policy (effective 2025-09-15, archived copy). 'All consumer-facing chatbots… must disclose to users that they are interacting with AI rather than a human… at a minimum at the beginning of each chat session.' 'High-Risk Use Cases' require that 'a qualified professional in that field must review the content or decision prior to dissemination', plus disclosure. They cover Legal, Healthcare (wellness excluded), Insurance, Finance, Employment and housing, Academic testing, and 'Media or professional journalistic content: automatically generate content and publish it for external consumption'. Products serving minors must follow additional guidelines. A later version may exist.

EU AI Act Article 50, SECONDARY (two 2026 sources agree): it applies from 2 August 2026 and was not deferred by the AI Omnibus, which entered into force on 27 July 2026 and moved Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027. Duties: tell people they are interacting with AI (50(1)); machine-readable marking of synthetic output (50(2)), with generative systems already on the market until 2 December 2026; deepfake disclosure (50(4)). Fines are up to €15M or 3% of turnover. An app that builds on a third-party model API is usually a deployer, and becomes a provider when it puts its own name on the system.

Korea AI Basic Act (in force 2026-01-22). art. 31(1): a business providing a product or service using generative AI must notify users in advance that it runs on AI. 31(2): outputs must be labelled as AI-generated. 31(3): hard-to-distinguish synthetic sound, image or video needs a clear notice. art. 4(1): the Act applies to acts abroad that affect the Korean market or users. art. 43(1)1: a fine of up to ₩30M for failing the art. 31(1) notice. art. 36: foreign businesses above thresholds set by Presidential Decree must appoint a domestic agent (thresholds not fetched).

Korea PIPA art. 28-8(1): personal information may be transferred abroad (including processing by an entrusted processor and storage) only with (1) separate consent, or (3) where needed for the contract, after disclosing the details in the privacy policy or notifying the user. art. 31-2: foreign processors above Decree thresholds must appoint a domestic agent. The mirrored text is the version promulgated 2026-09-08 and effective 2027-03-09.

Platform and search policies. Apple guideline 5.1.2(i) (effective 2025-11-13, secondary): an app must name the third-party AI provider and get explicit opt-in consent before sending it personal data. Google's 'scaled content abuse' spam policy applies to AI content regardless of method; the March 2026 core update reportedly cut traffic 50–80% for sites mass-publishing AI pages (search snippet). Chrome Web Store: a paid extension must make a trader declaration that publishes the legal name, phone and physical address.

Base rate (counter-evidence to any revenue plan): TrustMRR's n=5,079 Stripe-verified products have a year-0 median MRR of $148 and an overall median of $169. In a 2022 sample, more than 54% of tracked products earned $0. Among survivors, the median time to $1K MRR was 8 months.

conclusions: BOTTOM LINE ON PAYMENTS. With ≤3 owner-hours a week and customers worldwide, the only workable setup is a merchant of record (MoR) for web subscriptions and store billing for mobile apps. An MoR is a company that sells to the customer in its own name and handles the tax. For web, use Paddle or Polar, or Stripe Managed Payments if Stripe accepts the product. Do not start a new build on Lemon Squeezy. Plain Stripe fits only if sales are limited to Canada, and possibly the US. The deciding reason is foreign VAT, not Canadian GST/HST. The EU gives non-EU sellers no threshold, and Korea's VAT Act art. 53-2 requires registration within 20 days of starting, with no threshold in the statute, so both apply from the first consumer sale. Art. 53-2(2) makes a payment-collecting intermediary such as an MoR or app store the deemed supplier, and the EU has a similar rule (secondary). Canadian GST/HST, by contrast, does not apply until the owner passes $30k (s.148, s.166).

ESTIMATE, fees on C$5,000/month. Assumptions: price C$20, so 5,000 / 20 = 250 transactions; 60% of cards international; fixed fees treated as CAD. Stripe direct, domestic cards only: 3.6% × 5,000 + 0.30 × 250 = $255 (5.1%). Stripe direct plus Stripe Tax plus the international and FX surcharges: 4.1% × 5,000 + 75 + 0.6 × 5,000 × 2.8% = $364 (7.3%), and the owner still carries all foreign-VAT registrations. Paddle: 5% × 5,000 + 0.50 × 250 = $375 (7.5%). Polar Starter: 250 + 125 + 0.6 × 5,000 × 1.5% = $420 (8.4%), plus payout fees. Lemon Squeezy: 5.5% × 5,000 + 125 + 45 = $445 (8.9%). Stripe Managed Payments, domestic: 7.1% × 5,000 + 75 = $430 (8.6%); with the international surcharges, $514 (10.3%). App stores: $750 (15%), or $1,500 (30%) without the Small Business Program. An MoR costs roughly $100–$250/month more than plain Stripe at this volume, which is cheap compared with registering for VAT in the EU, UK and Korea. Price at US$/C$10 or more, because Paddle requires a custom discussion below $10.

PRODUCT-CATEGORY SCREEN, the most decision-relevant compliance finding. Several 'AI consultation bot' ideas fail on law or on payment and AI-provider policy, independent of market demand. (1) Paid immigration advice is an offence under IRPA s.91, with penalties up to $200k and 2 years on indictment. (2) Legal, health, finance, tax, insurance, employment/housing and exam advice are 'High-Risk' under Anthropic's Usage Policy, which requires a qualified professional to review before anything is released. That contradicts 'the owner does not intervene'. Polar also bans tax guidance and medical advice. (3) Fortune-telling (사주/tarot) and AI companions are prohibited by Polar's AUP, and other MoRs are unverified. (4) Games aimed at minors or using loot boxes are prohibited on Polar and add Anthropic's rules for products serving minors. (5) AI content sites that publish automatically are 'Media… automatically generate content and publish it' under Anthropic's policy, which also requires human review, and they face Google's scaled-content-abuse enforcement. Categories that pass the screen: adult productivity and utility tools, B2B micro-tools, language-practice tools that do not resell real exam questions, and adult casual games without gambling mechanics.

GST/HST TIMELINE (ESTIMATE). Assumed ramp: Nov 2026 $500, Dec $2,000, Jan 2027 $4,000, then $5,000/month. Q4 2026 = $2,500; Q1 2027 = $14,000; Q2 2027 = $15,000. The four quarters before Q2 2027 total 0 + 0 + 2,500 + 14,000 = $16,500, which is ≤ $30k, so the owner remains a small supplier through Q2 2027 and July 2027. The four quarters before Q3 2027 total 0 + 2,500 + 14,000 + 15,000 = $31,500, which is over $30k, so small-supplier status ends on 2027-08-01 and the registration application is due within 30 days (s.240(2.1)(b)). At the base-rate median (about $148/month), the threshold is never reached. Either way, GST/HST is not a launch task in the 2–3 month window. It becomes one when revenue reaches about $2,500/month on a sustained basis. Selling through an MoR, what counts toward the threshold is probably the amount the MoR owes the owner, but this depends on the contract and is unverified. After registration, a sale to a non-resident MoR is zero-rated only if that MoR is not normally GST-registered (Sch VI Part V ss.10/10.1). Ask the accountant which applies to the chosen MoR.

VOLUNTARY GST/HST REGISTRATION: not recommended for the 2–3 month horizon. ESTIMATE: if about $300/month of inputs carry 13% HST, the input tax credits come to about $39/month (0.13 × 300). That does not justify periodic filings plus a minimum 1-year registration (s.242(2)). If the owner sells directly with Stripe to Canadians after registering, they must charge by the customer's province: Ontario 13%. Rates for other provinces were not verified. Showing prices as 'plus applicable taxes' is allowed, because s.74.01(1.1) exempts amounts imposed by law, but any mandatory 'platform fee' must be included in the advertised price.

EI (this is the owner's largest money decision, and delegating the work to AI does NOT avoid it). EI Regs s.30(1) is triggered by operating a business on one's own account, whoever does the work. Only 'minor extent' (s.30(2)) keeps benefits flowing. The low time spent helps factor (a), but a business designed to earn $5k/month continuously counts against factors (c) and (d). JUDGMENT, not verified: it is unlikely to be treated as minor at the target scale. Subscription sales are allocated to the week of the transaction (s.36(6.1)(b)). ESTIMATE, using B = $729 and weekly insurable earnings of $1,325 (90% = $1,192.50), in the 'minor extent accepted' case. Net $1,000/month → $230.77/week → EI 729 − 115.38 = $613.62. Net $2,000/month → $461.54/week → EI $498.23. Net $4,000/month → $923.08/week → EI $267.46, total $1,190.54/week. EI reaches $0 at a net of about $1,325/week (about $5,743/month). If Service Canada rules the business is not minor, EI is $0 in every operating week. Early-stage revenue is realistically $0–$1,000/month (base rates), and at that level EI is worth far more than the business. So: file the EI claim by 2026-10-10 (Pilot 24 window), describe the planned online business to Service Canada before launch, and declare every week's net sales (s.38(1)(c) penalty risk). The AI can prepare the weekly EI earnings figure automatically from MoR payout data.

CASL DESIGN (the AI can implement all of this). (a) Sign-up form: an unchecked marketing-consent box that states the purpose, the sender's identity and the right to withdraw (s.10(1); SOR/2012-36 s.4). (b) Receipts, renewal notices and product-update emails are exempt from consent under s.6(6)(b), (d), (f), but must still identify the sender, give contact information and include an unsubscribe. (c) Paying subscribers give implied consent until 2 years after they cancel (s.10(10)(a), s.10(14)(a)). For free sign-ups, rely at most on the 6-month 'inquiry' window, and preferably on express consent. (d) No cold email to consumers. B2B cold email only to addresses conspicuously published with no 'no solicitation' notice, where the message is relevant to the person's role, with an evidence log (s.10(9)(b), s.13 onus). (e) Every commercial email needs a mailing address, so the owner should rent a virtual mailbox or PO box. The same address can serve for Chrome Web Store and app-store trader disclosures without exposing the home address. (f) CASL covers emails sent from Canada to foreign users (s.12(1)).

PIPEDA DESIGN FOR CHAT DATA. Show a purpose notice at the start of each chat; this can double as the AI disclosure. Collect only what the bot needs. Store chat logs only with the user's consent, and auto-delete them after a fixed period. The period is a design choice, since PIPEDA sets no number; 4.5.3 requires destroying information once it is no longer needed. Protect logs with encryption and access control proportionate to their sensitivity (4.7). Put the owner's processors (the Anthropic API, hosting, the MoR) under contract terms (4.1.3). Publish a privacy policy naming the owner as the accountable person with a contact address (4.8.2). Keep a breach log for 24 months. Avoid product categories that invite sensitive data such as health or immigration status. Serving Korean users adds PIPA art. 28-8 disclosure of overseas transfer. EU and Quebec users add GDPR and Law 25 [prior knowledge, unverified, pre-2026-06]. Restricting the target markets reduces this load.

AI DISCLOSURE, one implementation for all regimes: a 'You are chatting with an AI assistant (Claude)' notice at the start of every session, plus an 'AI-generated' label on outputs. This satisfies Anthropic's Usage Policy (disclose at the start of each session), EU AI Act Art. 50(1) (from 2026-08-02) and Korea AI Basic Act art. 31(1)–(2). Korea fines up to ₩30M for a missing notice. If the product generates images, audio or video for EU users, add machine-readable provenance such as C2PA/metadata (Art. 50(2)). If an iOS app sends personal data to Anthropic, Apple 5.1.2(i) requires an explicit opt-in that names the provider. Never present the bot as a human, and never generate testimonials or reviews: that breaches Competition Act s.74.01 (individual penalty up to $750k) and Polar's AUP.

REFUNDS AND CANCELLATION, one design meets the strictest regime found. Cancellation must be possible in the app or on the site, in no more steps than signup and by the same method (Korea art. 21-2(1)4; the EU withdrawal function; the Ontario and all-province ban on negative-option billing). Require consent and send notice before any free-to-paid conversion or price increase (Korea art. 13(6)). Offer a 14-day no-questions refund on the first payment, which matches the EU 14-day withdrawal right and avoids arguing the Korean digital-content exception (art. 17(2)5, 17(6)). Show the full price on the first screen, with taxes as the only add-on. The MoR processes the refunds, but the owner's own interface still has to meet these rules.

OWNER-TIME MAPPING (ESTIMATE, durations not sourced). LEGAL RESPONSIBILITY STAYS WITH THE OWNER. 'The AI does the work' does not transfer legal responsibility. The owner carries the CASL burden of proof (s.13), PIPEDA accountability (Sched. 1 4.1), Competition Act exposure, IRPA liability, the Anthropic AUP obligations, the MoR's acceptable-use and chargeback limits (Polar can suspend at about 0.7% chargebacks), and EI disclosure. The Routines should include guardrails: no outbound marketing email without a logged consent basis; a banned-category filter on anything the AI builds; an automatic AI disclosure; and a weekly compliance report that the owner approves.

COUNTER-EVIDENCE AND HONEST FRAMING. Compliance is not the binding constraint; distribution is. The year-0 median MRR is $148 and more than 54% of products earn $0 (cand_saas.json). The MoR-versus-Stripe difference is about 2–3% of revenue. The choice that decides whether money arrives at all is product and channel. MoRs add risks of their own: account review or refusal (Polar marks AI content tools and chatbot generators for closer review), discretionary refunds for up to 60 days (Polar), payout fees and foreign-exchange costs, and a first Stripe payout 7–14 days after the first sale. Cash from any launch in October 2026 therefore realistically arrives in November at the earliest.
